tagline: Forking copies the transcript into a **new session** — the original is never touched.
summary: A Claude Code session is a **transcript**: every message, tool call, and result, stored under a session ID. Forking that session makes a **full copy under a new ID**. The copy and the original then **diverge independently** — nothing you do in one ever shows up in the other.

sections.heading: Three ways back into a session
body: **--continue** reopens your **most recent session** in place — same session ID, the transcript just keeps growing. **--resume** lets you **pick which session** to reopen (interactively or by ID); by default it also continues that session in place.

**--fork-session** changes what resume does: instead of growing the original, Claude Code **copies the transcript into a new session ID** and continues there. The original stays exactly as you left it — a safe point you can return to or fork again.

sections.heading: Rewind is time travel, not forking
body: Inside a session, **rewind** (double-Escape or /rewind) jumps the conversation — and optionally your code — **back to an earlier checkpoint**. That rewrites where the session continues from, but it is still **one session, one transcript**. Forking creates a **second transcript**; rewinding moves within the one you have.
The two compose: rewind to the turn where things were still good, then **fork from there** to try a different approach while keeping the original line of work intact.

diagram.caption: One transcript, two ways to pick it back up: **in place** (it grows) or **as a copy** (the original is frozen and safe).

nodes.label: Conversation so far
nodes.note: Every turn so far lives in **one transcript** under **one session ID** — this is the thing that gets continued or copied.

nodes.label: Pick it back up — how?
nodes.note: **--continue** grabs the most recent session; **--resume** lets you choose one. Adding **--fork-session** turns either into a **copy operation**.

nodes.label: Same session grows
nodes.note: Without forking, new turns are **appended to the original transcript**. There is still only **one session**.

nodes.label: Copy under a new session ID
nodes.note: **--fork-session** copies the whole transcript into a **new session ID**. New turns land in the **copy**.

nodes.label: Two independent transcripts
nodes.note: The fork and the original are now **fully independent**. Neither sees the other's new turns. The original is a **safe restore point**.

scenarios.title: Pick up the **most recent session** with --continue
scenarios.note: No copy is made. The session you left is the session you're in — **same ID, same transcript**, now longer.

scenarios.title: Fork a session to **try something risky**
scenarios.note: The fork gets **everything the original had** at the moment of forking — then they **diverge**. Abandon the fork and the original is exactly as you left it.

misconceptions.myth: Forking a session keeps some link back to the original — work in the fork eventually shows up there too.
misconceptions.reality: A fork is a **copy**, not a branch of a shared thing. From the moment of forking, the two transcripts are **completely independent** — no merging, no syncing, no link.
misconceptions.why: Git trains you to expect branches to merge back. Conversation forks have no merge — the word 'fork' is doing different work here.

misconceptions.reality: **--continue** always reopens the **most recent** session. **--resume** lets you **choose** which session — and is where **--fork-session** usually comes in.
misconceptions.why: They feel the same when you only have one recent session. The difference appears the day you have several and continue grabs the wrong one.
